idiom_name: std::chrono::year_month_day bounds + std::optional end + a contains() free function
implementation_notes: C++20 supplies a real calendar date type: std::chrono::year_month_day is a field type with operator<=> and an implicit conversion to std::chrono::sys_days for day arithmetic, so the classic Range class collapses into a two-member struct (or a std::pair) plus a free contains(). Use std::optional<year_month_day> for "until further notice" instead of a sentinel date, and year_month_day::ok() to reject invalid bounds at construction. The classic hand-written Date/Range classes are still justified only on pre-C++20 toolchains or when bounds must follow a non-Gregorian calendar.
pitfalls: year_month_day is a field type: it adds years and months directly, but day arithmetic only after conversion to sys_days, and ymd + std::chrono::months(1) can produce a date whose ok() is false (31 January + one month).
A default-constructed year_month_day has uninitialised fields; comparisons against it are meaningless - always construct bounds explicitly and route user input through ok().
An empty period (until == from) compares as valid: decide whether an empty validity period is a domain error and assert it in the constructor.

variants.name: Boost.Date_Time date_period (pre-C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++20 the period type comes from a library: boost::gregorian::date_period constructs [begin, end), exposes contains(date), contains(period), intersects(period) and intersection(period) - exactly the operations this pattern needs - and Howard Hinnant's date.h provides the calendar date type for C++11/14/17 toolchains. Effectivity then holds one date_period per dated fact and answers as-of questions with contains(). Choose this variant while the toolchain is pre-C++20 or when the codebase already uses Boost.Date_Time; the C++20 variant is preferable as soon as the standard calendar types are available, because it removes the dependency.
pitfalls: date_period is half-open and treats end <= begin as an invalid (null) period rather than throwing, so an accidentally inverted range silently contains nothing - assert is_null() == false after construction.
An open end must be modelled outside the period type: use a far-future bound consistently or keep an explicit "open" flag beside it; a Date::max() sentinel leaks into length arithmetic.
Howard Hinnant's date.h keeps sys_days (absolute) and local_days (zone-dependent) apart; converting user input through the wrong one shifts the boundary by a day.
